category.name: Biology
category.tagline: Organelles to action potentials: the mechanisms, numbers and traps biology exams test.

packs.title: Cell Structure & Membranes
packs.description: Organelle jobs, endosymbiosis evidence, the cytoskeleton, the fluid mosaic membrane, tonicity, passive vs active transport, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and junctions.

cards.title: In a prokaryotic cell, what is the region called where the DNA is concentrated without any membrane around it?
cards.body:
The nucleoid.
Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes enclose their DNA in a nucleus bounded by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores.

cards.title: Which dense, non-membrane-bound region inside the nucleus makes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits?
cards.body:
The nucleolus.
rRNA made there is combined with proteins imported from the cytoplasm into large and small subunits, which exit through nuclear pores. A large and a small subunit join into a working ribosome only in the cytoplasm.

cards.title: Proteins headed for mitochondria, chloroplasts or the nucleus: are they made on free ribosomes or on ER-bound ribosomes?
cards.body:
Free ribosomes in the cytosol.
Free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins and proteins imported later into mitochondria, chloroplasts and the nucleus. ER-bound ribosomes make secreted proteins (e.g., insulin), membrane proteins, and proteins for the ER, Golgi and lysosomes. The ribosomes are identical; a signal peptide on the new protein sends a ribosome to the ER.

cards.title: Which organelle makes lipids such as steroid hormones, detoxifies drugs in liver cells, and stores Ca²⁺ in muscle cells?
cards.body:
Smooth ER (no ribosomes).
Drugs such as barbiturates and alcohol make liver cells build more smooth ER, which raises drug tolerance. In muscle, its release of Ca²⁺ triggers contraction. Rough ER, studded with ribosomes, makes secretory and membrane proteins instead.

cards.title: Which face of the Golgi apparatus receives the transport vesicles arriving from the ER?
cards.body:
The cis face (the receiving side, near the ER).
Products are modified as they pass through the cisternae (e.g., glycoprotein carbohydrates trimmed and altered, phosphate ID tags added), then sorted into vesicles that leave from the trans face (the shipping side).

cards.title: In an animal cell, which membrane-bound sac of hydrolytic enzymes digests engulfed food and recycles worn-out organelles?
cards.body:
The lysosome.
Its enzymes work best at about pH 5, kept acidic by H⁺ pumps in its membrane; enzymes that leak out do little at the cytosol's near-neutral pH. Recycling organelles is called autophagy. In Tay-Sachs disease a lipid-digesting lysosomal enzyme is missing, so lipids build up in brain cells.

cards.title: Which organelle transfers hydrogen from substrates to O₂, producing H₂O₂ that its own enzyme then converts to water?
cards.body:
The peroxisome.
These reactions break fatty acids into smaller molecules that mitochondria burn as fuel and, in liver cells, detoxify alcohol. The enzyme catalase turns the toxic H₂O₂ into H₂O. Glyoxysomes, specialized peroxisomes in fat-storing seeds, help convert fatty acids to sugar.

cards.title: Give three lines of evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from engulfed prokaryotes.
cards.body:
Any three: a double membrane; their own circular DNA without histones, like a bacterial chromosome; their own ribosomes, which resemble bacterial ribosomes (including antibiotic sensitivity); division by a process like binary fission; inner-membrane enzymes and transport systems like those of prokaryotes.
Mitochondria came from an alphaproteobacterium, chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium.

cards.title: Which cytoskeletal fibers resist compression, form the mitotic spindle, and make up the core of cilia and flagella?
cards.body:
Microtubules: hollow tubes of tubulin dimers, ≈25 nm wide, the thickest fibers.
In animal cells they grow out from the centrosome, and motor proteins carry vesicles along them. Motile cilia and flagella have a 9 + 2 pattern (nine doublets around two single microtubules), bent by dynein motors.

cards.title: Which cytoskeletal fibers form the animal cleavage furrow and the core of microvilli, and work with myosin to contract muscle?
cards.body:
Microfilaments (actin filaments), ≈7 nm wide, the thinnest fibers.
They bear tension and power amoeboid movement and cytoplasmic streaming. Don't confuse them with intermediate filaments (8–12 nm; e.g., keratins, nuclear lamins), the most permanent fibers, which anchor the nucleus and other organelles in place.

cards.title: In the fluid mosaic model of a cell membrane, what is 'fluid' and what makes up the 'mosaic'?
cards.body:
Fluid: phospholipids (and many proteins) drift sideways within the bilayer, though flip-flopping across it is rare. Mosaic: many different proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer.
Unsaturated, kinked fatty acid tails keep membranes fluid in the cold; in animal cells, cholesterol buffers fluidity against temperature changes.

cards.title: What happens to an animal cell and to a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution? In a hypertonic one?
cards.body:
Hypotonic (water moves in): the animal cell swells and may lyse; the plant cell becomes turgid, its healthy state, as the wall pushes back.
Hypertonic (water moves out): the animal cell shrivels; the plant cell plasmolyzes as its membrane pulls away from the wall.
In isotonic solution the animal cell is normal but the plant cell is flaccid (limp).

cards.title: Glucose enters a red blood cell down its concentration gradient via a carrier protein, using no ATP. What kind of transport is this?
cards.body:
Facilitated diffusion, a form of passive transport.
Using a transport protein doesn't make it active: the energy comes from the gradient itself. Active transport moves solutes against their gradient and needs energy, from ATP or from another solute's gradient (cotransport).

cards.title: For each ATP it uses, how many Na⁺ and K⁺ ions does the sodium-potassium pump move, and in which directions?
cards.body:
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, both against their concentration gradients (active transport).
ATP phosphorylates the pump, changing its shape. Because each cycle exports one net positive charge, it is an electrogenic pump that adds to the negative charge inside the cell.

cards.title: Cells take in LDL particles bound to specific proteins clustered in coated pits, which pinch inward. What type of endocytosis is this?
cards.body:
Receptor-mediated endocytosis.
The coated pit forms a coated vesicle carrying the LDL inside. In familial hypercholesterolemia, defective or missing LDL receptors leave LDL in the blood, causing early atherosclerosis. Other endocytosis: phagocytosis (cell eating) and pinocytosis (cell drinking). Exocytosis does the reverse, secreting vesicle contents.

cards.title: Which animal cell junctions are protein-lined pores letting ions and small molecules pass straight between cells, as in heart muscle?
cards.body:
Gap junctions.
Plant cells use plasmodesmata, channels through their cell walls. Other animal junctions: tight junctions press membranes together into a seal that blocks leakage (e.g., between skin cells); desmosomes are rivets, anchored by intermediate filaments, that fasten cells into strong sheets.

packs.title: Cell Cycle, Mitosis & Meiosis
packs.description: Cell-cycle phases, mitosis stages, chromosome counts, meiosis I vs II, crossing over, nondisjunction, checkpoints, MPF, p53 and oncogenes vs tumor suppressors.

cards.title: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA replicated?
cards.body:
S phase (synthesis).
Order: G1 → S → G2 → M. G1, S and G2 together make up interphase, often about 90% of the cycle, and the cell grows throughout it. The M phase is mitosis plus cytokinesis.

cards.title: A human body cell has finished S phase and is now in G2. How many chromosomes does it contain?
cards.body:
46, made up of 92 sister chromatids.
Replication doubles the DNA but not the chromosome number: each chromosome now has two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, so count centromeres. The count briefly doubles to 92 only in anaphase, when sisters separate.

cards.title: List the five stages of mitosis in order.
cards.body:
Prophase → prometaphase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase.
Cytokinesis usually overlaps the end of telophase. Some texts fold prometaphase into prophase and list only four stages (PMAT).

cards.title: In which stage of mitosis does the nuclear envelope fragment, letting spindle microtubules reach and attach to the chromosomes?
cards.body:
Prometaphase.
Each chromatid now has a kinetochore, and kinetochore microtubules start moving the chromosomes toward the cell's midline. Four-stage schemes call this late prophase.

cards.title: What protein structure forms at the centromere of each sister chromatid and is where spindle microtubules attach?
cards.body:
The kinetochore.
Don't mix up: centromere = the DNA region where sister chromatids are most tightly joined; centrosome = the microtubule-organizing center at each spindle pole (with a pair of centrioles in animal cells); kinetochore = the attachment site for spindle microtubules.

cards.title: During cytokinesis in a plant cell, what structure forms from fused Golgi-derived vesicles and develops into the new cell wall?
cards.body:
The cell plate.
A rigid wall means plant cells can't pinch in two. Animal cells instead form a cleavage furrow: a contractile ring of actin microfilaments, interacting with myosin, tightens until the cell splits.

cards.title: Which meiotic division separates homologous chromosomes, and which separates sister chromatids?
cards.body:
Meiosis I separates homologs (the reductional division: diploid → haploid). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis.
In humans, one 2n = 46 cell gives two cells with 23 duplicated chromosomes after meiosis I, then four haploid cells with 23 chromosomes each.

cards.title: When during meiosis does crossing over occur, and between which chromatids?
cards.body:
Prophase I, between nonsister chromatids of a homologous pair held together in synapsis.
The X-shaped sites where it has happened are chiasmata. It creates recombinant chromosomes that combine maternal and paternal alleles.

cards.title: Independent orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I alone allows how many chromosome combinations in human gametes?
cards.body:
2²³, about 8.4 million (23 pairs, each able to line up 2 ways).
Random fertilization then allows about 70 trillion (2²³ × 2²³) zygote combinations, before crossing over adds even more variation.

cards.title: If nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I vs meiosis II, what fraction of the resulting gametes is abnormal in each case?
cards.body:
Meiosis I: all four gametes are abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: half are (one n + 1, one n − 1, two normal).
An n + 1 gamete fused with a normal one gives a trisomic zygote (2n + 1); an n − 1 gamete gives a monosomic one (2n − 1).

cards.title: Down syndrome usually results from having three copies of which chromosome?
cards.body:
Chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), usually from nondisjunction; the risk rises with maternal age.
Sex-chromosome examples: XXY is Klinefelter syndrome (male); XO is Turner syndrome (female), the only known viable monosomy in humans.

cards.title: Which checkpoint is the key 'go/no-go' decision for many cells, after which the cell usually completes the whole cycle?
cards.body:
The G1 checkpoint (called the restriction point in mammalian cells).
Without a go-ahead signal such as a growth factor, the cell exits into G0, a nondividing state. Most body cells are in G0; mature nerve and muscle cells never divide, but liver cells can be called back into the cycle after injury.

cards.title: What must be true before the M-phase (spindle) checkpoint lets a cell begin anaphase?
cards.body:
Every chromosome must be attached to spindle microtubules at its kinetochores, with sister kinetochores attached to opposite poles, and aligned at the metaphase plate.
Any unattached kinetochore delays anaphase, which keeps daughter cells from getting missing or extra chromosomes.

cards.title: Which cyclin–Cdk complex, once enough accumulates in late G2, triggers the cell's passage past the G2 checkpoint into M phase?
cards.body:
MPF (maturation-promoting factor, also called M-phase-promoting factor).
Cdk levels stay fairly constant; cyclin builds up during S and G2 and activates Cdk. During anaphase, MPF switches itself off by triggering the breakdown of its own cyclin.

cards.title: Which tumor-suppressor protein, nicknamed the 'guardian of the genome', halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged?
cards.body:
p53.
This transcription factor switches on p21 (which binds Cdks and stops the cycle), DNA-repair genes, and, if the damage can't be fixed, genes that trigger apoptosis. The p53 gene is mutated in roughly half of all human cancers.

cards.title: Why is one mutated allele of a proto-oncogene enough to promote cancer, while tumor-suppressor genes usually need both alleles lost?
cards.body: Proto-oncogene mutations are gain of function: one hyperactive allele (now an oncogene, e.g., ras) is enough, like a stuck accelerator. Tumor-suppressor mutations are loss of function: one working allele still makes enough protein, so both copies must be lost (e.g., p53, BRCA1), like failed brakes. Cancer usually needs several such mutations.

packs.title: DNA, RNA & Protein Synthesis
packs.description: Base pairing, Chargaff's rules, replication enzymes, Okazaki fragments, telomerase, transcription, RNA processing, codons, ribosome sites, mutations, operons.

cards.title: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C base pair together?
cards.body:
Three (A–T pairs have two), so GC-rich DNA needs more heat to separate.
Each pair joins a purine (A, G) with a pyrimidine (C, T; U in RNA), keeping the helix a uniform 2 nm wide. The two strands are antiparallel: they run 5′→3′ in opposite directions.

cards.title: A double-stranded DNA sample is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
cards.body:
20%.
Chargaff's rules: A = T and G = C. If A = 30%, T = 30%, leaving 40% for G + C, so G = 20% and C = 20%. This works only for double-stranded DNA.

cards.title: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on ¹⁵N, then moved them to ¹⁴N. Their results supported which model of DNA replication?
cards.body:
Semiconservative: each new double helix has one parental strand and one newly made strand.
After one round in ¹⁴N, all the DNA formed a single hybrid band (ruling out conservative); after two rounds, hybrid and light bands (ruling out dispersive).

cards.title: Which enzyme relieves the overwinding strain ahead of a replication fork by breaking, swiveling and rejoining DNA strands?
cards.body:
Topoisomerase.
Don't confuse it with helicase, which untwists the double helix at the fork, separating the two strands. Single-strand binding proteins then keep the separated strands from re-pairing.

cards.title: DNA polymerase can't start a new strand from scratch. Which enzyme synthesizes the short RNA starter that it extends?
cards.body:
Primase.
It makes an RNA primer (typically 5–10 nucleotides) whose free 3′ end gives DNA polymerase a start: polymerases can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end, so new DNA grows 5′→3′. The leading strand needs one primer; the lagging strand needs one for each Okazaki fragment.

cards.title: On the lagging strand in E. coli, what do DNA pol III, DNA pol I and DNA ligase each do?
cards.body:
DNA pol III extends each RNA primer into an Okazaki fragment. DNA pol I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA. DNA ligase seals the remaining nick, joining the sugar-phosphate backbones of adjacent fragments.
The strand is discontinuous because polymerase builds only 5′→3′, which on this strand means working away from the fork.

cards.title: Which enzyme lengthens the ends of linear chromosomes in germ cells, using an RNA template it carries with it?
cards.body:
Telomerase.
Once the RNA primer at the very end of a new strand is removed, it can't be replaced with DNA (no 3′ end to extend), so chromosomes shorten each round. Telomeres (TTAGGG repeats in humans) buffer this loss. Telomerase is active in germ cells and many cancer cells but not in most somatic cells.

cards.title: An mRNA has the same sequence (with U in place of T) as which DNA strand?
cards.body:
The coding (nontemplate) strand.
RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and builds a complementary RNA 5′→3′, so the RNA matches the other strand. Trap: the template strand is complementary to the mRNA, not identical to it.

cards.title: In eukaryotic promoters, what sequence ≈25 nucleotides upstream of the start point is a key binding site for transcription factors?
cards.body:
The TATA box.
Transcription factors bind it first, then RNA polymerase II joins them to form the transcription initiation complex. Unlike bacterial RNA polymerase, eukaryotic RNA polymerase can't recognize a promoter on its own.

cards.title: Name the three modifications that turn eukaryotic pre-mRNA into mature mRNA before it leaves the nucleus.
cards.body:
A 5′ cap (a modified guanine nucleotide), a poly-A tail (50–250 adenine nucleotides on the 3′ end), and RNA splicing, in which spliceosomes cut out introns and join the exons.
The cap and tail help export the mRNA from the nucleus, protect it from hydrolytic enzymes, and help ribosomes attach.

cards.title: Which codon starts translation, and which three codons stop it?
cards.body:
Start: AUG, which also codes for methionine and sets the reading frame.
Stop: UAA, UAG, UGA. They code for no amino acid; a protein release factor binds the stop codon in the A site and frees the polypeptide.
Mnemonic: U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away.

cards.title: An mRNA codon reads 5′-GCA-3′. What is the matching tRNA anticodon, written 5′→3′?
cards.body:
5′-UGC-3′.
Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel: 5′-GCA-3′ pairs with 3′-CGU-5′, which reads UGC when written 5′→3′. Trap: answering CGU without flipping it. GCA codes for alanine, so this tRNA carries Ala.

cards.title: During elongation, what does each tRNA binding site on the ribosome (A, P and E) hold?
cards.body:
A site: the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA with the next amino acid. P site: the tRNA holding the growing polypeptide. E site: the empty tRNA about to exit.
The polypeptide is transferred onto the A-site amino acid (rRNA catalyzes the peptide bond), then the ribosome shifts one codon so tRNAs move A → P → E.

cards.title: Inserting or deleting nucleotides in a number that isn't a multiple of three causes what type of mutation?
cards.body:
A frameshift mutation: every codon after it is misread, usually giving a nonfunctional protein, often cut short by an early stop codon.
Substitution types: silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid, e.g., sickle-cell disease), nonsense (codon becomes a stop codon).

cards.title: What is the natural inducer of the lac operon, the molecule that binds and inactivates the lac repressor?
cards.body:
Allolactose, an isomer of lactose (trap: not lactose itself; IPTG is a synthetic lab inducer).
The lac operon is inducible: usually off because the repressor sits on the operator. When glucose is scarce, cAMP builds up and activates CAP, which helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter and boosts transcription (positive control).

cards.title: How does abundant tryptophan switch off the trp operon in E. coli?
cards.body:
It acts as a corepressor: tryptophan binds the trp repressor, which is inactive on its own, and activates it, so the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.
The trp operon is repressible (usually on; anabolic pathway). The lac operon is inducible (usually off; catabolic pathway).

packs.title: Mendelian & Population Genetics
packs.description: Mendel's laws, cross ratios and probability, testcrosses, dominance, ABO, epistasis, X-linkage, pedigrees, map units, Hardy–Weinberg math and drift.

cards.title: Which of Mendel's laws says the two alleles for a character separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets just one?
cards.body:
The law of segregation.
Its physical basis: homologous chromosomes, which carry the two alleles, separate in anaphase I of meiosis. So a heterozygote (Aa) makes A and a gametes in a 1:1 ratio.

cards.title: In a Pp × Pp cross (purple dominant to white), what fraction of the purple-flowered offspring are heterozygous?
cards.body:
2/3.
Genotypes come out 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so phenotypes are 3 purple : 1 white. Of the 3 purple, 2 are Pp. Trap: 1/2 is the fraction of all offspring that are Pp.

cards.title: How can you find out whether a purple-flowered pea plant (dominant phenotype) is PP or Pp?
cards.body:
A testcross: breed it with a homozygous recessive (pp, white) plant.
All purple offspring → the plant is PP. About half white (1:1) → it's Pp. The pp parent can only pass on p, so each offspring's phenotype reveals which allele the unknown parent gave.

cards.title: What phenotypic ratio comes from an AaBb × AaBb cross with two unlinked genes, each showing complete dominance?
cards.body:
9:3:3:1 (9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb).
Each gene alone gives 3:1, and (3:1) × (3:1) = 9:3:3:1. This is the signature of independent assortment; linkage or epistasis changes it.

cards.title: With three unlinked genes, what fraction of the offspring from AaBbCc × AaBbCc will be aabbcc?
cards.body:
1/64, by the product rule: each gene independently gives 1/4 homozygous recessive, so 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64.
Use the sum rule (add) when an outcome can arise in more than one mutually exclusive way: Aa from Aa × Aa = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

cards.title: Red snapdragons crossed with white ones give all pink offspring. What inheritance pattern explains this?
cards.body:
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype.
Crossing two pinks gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio. It isn't blending, since red and white reappear. Contrast codominance, where both alleles show fully (e.g., AB blood type).

cards.title: A type A parent and a type B parent have a type O child. What are the parents' genotypes?
cards.body:
Iᴬi and Iᴮi (both heterozygous); the child is ii.
Their children could be AB, A, B or O, each with probability 1/4. ABO has three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant (type AB shows both A and B carbohydrates), and both are dominant to i.

cards.title: Labradors with genotype ee are yellow no matter which B/b alleles they carry. What is this kind of gene interaction called?
cards.body:
Epistasis: the E gene (whether pigment is deposited in fur) masks the B gene (black vs brown pigment).
BbEe × BbEe gives 9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow instead of 9:3:3:1.

cards.title: A woman who carries an X-linked recessive allele has children with an unaffected man. What fraction of their sons will be affected?
cards.body:
1/2: each son gets one of his mother's two X chromosomes (and his father's Y).
No daughters are affected, but half are carriers. Males need only one copy because they're hemizygous, so disorders like hemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are far more common in males.

cards.title: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. What mode of inheritance must the trait have?
cards.body:
Autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers (heterozygous).
It can't be dominant: an affected child would need an affected parent. It can't be X-linked recessive: an affected daughter would need an affected father.

cards.title: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes. What kind of genes tend to break it?
cards.body:
Linked genes: genes close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together.
Only crossing over separates them, producing recombinant offspring. Genes far apart on one chromosome recombine so often (up to 50%) that they assort as if unlinked.
acceptedAnswers: genes close together on the same chromosome

cards.title: A testcross yields 2,000 offspring, 160 of them recombinant for two genes. How far apart are the genes on a linkage map?
cards.body:
8 map units (centimorgans).
Recombination frequency = 160 ÷ 2,000 = 8%, and 1% recombination = 1 map unit (1 cM). Genes farther apart cross over more often. Frequencies top out at 50%, and map units measure crossover frequency, not physical distance.

cards.title: Write the two Hardy–Weinberg equations and say what each term stands for.
cards.body:
p + q = 1: allele frequencies (p = dominant allele, q = recessive allele).
p² + 2pq + q² = 1: genotype frequencies (p² = homozygous dominant, 2pq = heterozygous, q² = homozygous recessive).

cards.title: List the five conditions a population must meet to stay in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
cards.body:
1) No mutations. 2) Random mating. 3) No natural selection. 4) An extremely large population (no genetic drift). 5) No gene flow.
If any is violated, allele or genotype frequencies can change from generation to generation.

cards.title: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 newborns. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg, about what fraction of people are carriers?
cards.body:
About 2% (≈1 in 50).
q² = 0.0001, so q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. Carriers = 2pq = 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 ≈ 0.0198. Traps: using q² or q as the carrier frequency, or forgetting to take the square root.

cards.title: A few individuals colonize an island, and by chance a rare mainland allele becomes common there. Which kind of genetic drift is this?
cards.body:
The founder effect, a form of genetic drift.
The small founding group's allele frequencies differ from the source population's by chance. Related: the bottleneck effect, when a disaster or habitat loss drastically shrinks a population, as with Illinois's greater prairie chickens. Drift is strongest in small populations.

packs.title: Respiration & Photosynthesis
packs.description: Enzymes and inhibitors, glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, the ETC and chemiosmosis, ATP yield, fermentation, light reactions, the Calvin cycle, C4 and CAM.

cards.title: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by lowering what?
cards.body:
The activation energy (EA), the energy needed to reach the transition state.
Enzymes don't change ΔG, so they can't make an endergonic reaction spontaneous; they only speed up reactions that would happen anyway. They aren't used up and are specific to their substrates.

cards.title: An enzyme inhibitor's effect can be overcome by adding more substrate. What type of inhibitor is it?
cards.body:
A competitive inhibitor: it resembles the substrate and competes for the active site.
A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes its shape, making the active site less effective, so extra substrate doesn't help.

cards.title: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
cards.body:
2 ATP (4 made by substrate-level phosphorylation, minus 2 invested early on).
Glycolysis also yields 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate. It runs in the cytosol and doesn't need O₂.

cards.title: Pyruvate oxidation converts each pyruvate into what molecule, which then enters the citric acid cycle?
cards.body:
Acetyl CoA.
In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate loses a carbon as CO₂, the remaining two-carbon fragment is oxidized (NAD⁺ → NADH), and coenzyme A is attached. Per glucose: 2 acetyl CoA, 2 CO₂, 2 NADH.

cards.title: Per glucose (two turns), what does the citric acid cycle produce?
cards.body:
2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 4 CO₂ (per turn: 1 ATP, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 2 CO₂).
It runs in the mitochondrial matrix. With pyruvate oxidation's 2 CO₂, all six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂. In some cells, the cycle's one substrate-level phosphorylation step makes GTP instead of ATP.

cards.title: What is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
cards.body:
O₂, which picks up electrons and H⁺ to form water.
The chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae). Without O₂ the chain stalls, NADH can't be reoxidized, and cells must rely on fermentation. Cyanide kills by blocking electron transfer to O₂.

cards.title: In mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps H⁺ out of the matrix into which compartment?
cards.body:
The intermembrane space.
H⁺ flows back down its gradient into the matrix through ATP synthase, which uses this proton-motive force to make ATP from ADP and phosphate. This is chemiosmosis; together with the ETC it forms oxidative phosphorylation, which makes almost 90% of respiration's ATP.

cards.title: About how many ATP does aerobic respiration yield per glucose, and why isn't it an exact whole number?
cards.body:
About 30–32 ATP in current textbooks (older ones say 36–38).
Each NADH gives ≈2.5 ATP and each FADH₂ ≈1.5; NADH from glycolysis yields less if a shuttle passes its electrons to FAD; and some of the proton-motive force powers other work. That captures roughly a third of glucose's chemical energy.

cards.title: Fermentation makes no ATP beyond glycolysis. So what does it accomplish for a cell without O₂?
cards.body:
It regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH, so glycolysis (net 2 ATP per glucose) can keep running.
Lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate → lactate (muscle cells, some bacteria). Alcohol fermentation: pyruvate → CO₂ + acetaldehyde → ethanol (yeast).

cards.title: The O₂ released by photosynthesis comes from splitting which molecule?
cards.body:
Water (H₂O).
Photosystem II splits water to replace electrons lost by its P680 reaction center; the H⁺ goes into the thylakoid space and O₂ is released. ¹⁸O tracer experiments confirmed it: labeled water gives labeled O₂, labeled CO₂ doesn't. CO₂'s oxygen ends up in sugar and new water.

cards.title: In linear electron flow, which photosystem is the first to absorb light and pass electrons down the chain?
cards.body:
Photosystem II (reaction center P680); the photosystems are numbered in order of discovery.
Its electrons pass via an electron transport chain (plastoquinone → cytochrome complex → plastocyanin) to photosystem I (P700), then to NADP⁺, forming NADPH. The H⁺ gradient built along the way drives ATP synthesis. All of this happens in the thylakoid membranes.

cards.title: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
cards.body:
The stroma, the fluid surrounding the thylakoids.
It spends the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes. Location trap: thylakoid = light reactions, stroma = Calvin cycle (just as the mitochondrial matrix holds the citric acid cycle).

cards.title: Which enzyme catalyzes carbon fixation, the first step of the Calvin cycle, and is probably the most abundant protein on Earth?
cards.body:
Rubisco (RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase).
It attaches CO₂ to the 5-carbon sugar RuBP; the unstable 6-carbon product immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate. Rubisco can also bind O₂ instead of CO₂, which causes photorespiration.

cards.title: To make one net G3P from 3 CO₂, how many ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle use?
cards.body:
9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
Phases: carbon fixation (rubisco), reduction (6 ATP and 6 NADPH turn 3-phosphoglycerate into G3P), and regeneration of RuBP (3 ATP). The equivalent of one glucose takes 2 G3P: 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

cards.title: On hot, dry days a C3 plant closes its stomata, and rubisco starts adding O₂ instead of CO₂ to RuBP. What is this wasteful process?
cards.body:
Photorespiration.
It consumes O₂ and releases CO₂ but makes no ATP and no sugar, and can drain as much as 50% of the carbon fixed by the Calvin cycle. C3 crops such as rice, wheat and soybeans are vulnerable; C4 and CAM plants minimize it.

cards.title: How do C4 plants and CAM plants each keep initial CO₂ fixation separate from the Calvin cycle?
cards.body:
C4 (corn, sugarcane): in space. PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into 4-carbon compounds in mesophyll cells, which pass them to bundle-sheath cells that release CO₂ to the Calvin cycle.
CAM (cacti, pineapple): in time. Stomata open at night and CO₂ is stored as organic acids; by day, with stomata closed, the same cells release it to the Calvin cycle.

packs.title: Evolution & Speciation
packs.description: Natural selection, fitness, modes of selection, sexual selection, gene flow, homology, species concepts, reproductive barriers, speciation and cladistics.

cards.title: What conditions must hold for natural selection to change a population over generations?
cards.body:
Individuals vary in a trait; the variation is heritable; more offspring are produced than can survive and reproduce; and some heritable traits improve survival and reproduction.
Favored heritable traits then become more common over generations. Selection acts on individuals' phenotypes, but populations are what evolve.

cards.title: A strong, long-lived male mouse never fathers any offspring. What is his relative fitness?
cards.body:
Zero.
Relative fitness is an individual's contribution to the gene pool of the next generation compared with others' contributions. Strength and survival count only insofar as they lead to reproduction.

cards.title: After a drought left mostly large, hard seeds, finches with deeper beaks survived and mean beak depth rose. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Directional selection: individuals at one extreme are favored, shifting the population's mean.
This happened to medium ground finches on Daphne Major in the Galápagos after the 1977 drought: the survivors' offspring had deeper beaks on average.

cards.title: Babies of intermediate birth weight have historically survived better than very small or very large ones. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Stabilizing selection: it favors intermediate phenotypes and acts against both extremes, reducing variation while the mean stays put.
Most human birth weights fall around 3–4 kg; much smaller or larger babies have had higher mortality.

cards.title: Seedcracker finches with small or large beaks feed efficiently, but those with intermediate beaks don't. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Disruptive selection: both extremes are favored over intermediates, which can split the trait into two peaks.
In black-bellied seedcrackers in Cameroon, small-billed birds feed mainly on soft seeds and large-billed birds crack hard ones; intermediate bills handle both poorly.

cards.title: Peahens prefer to mate with the males that have the showiest tails. What specific form of sexual selection is this?
cards.body:
Intersexual selection (mate choice): members of one sex, usually females, choose mates based on certain traits.
Contrast intrasexual selection: competition within one sex, often males, for mates. Either can spread traits that boost mating success even if they reduce survival, producing sexual dimorphism.

cards.title: What is the movement of alleles into or out of a population by migrating fertile individuals or their gametes, such as pollen, called?
cards.body:
Gene flow.
It tends to make populations more genetically alike. It can spread useful alleles (e.g., insecticide resistance among mosquito populations) or swamp local adaptations. Contrast genetic drift: chance changes in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.

cards.title: How do homologous structures differ from analogous structures? Give an example of each.
cards.body:
Homologous: similar because of shared ancestry, even if their functions differ (human arm, whale flipper and bat wing share the same set of bones). Analogous: similar function but evolved independently by convergent evolution (bird wings vs insect wings).
Homologies indicate common ancestry; analogies don't.

cards.title: Remnants of structures that were functional in an organism's ancestors, like the pelvic bones of some snakes, are called what?
cards.body:
Vestigial structures.
They persist because they're inherited from ancestors that used them, so they're evidence of descent with modification. They may keep minor uses; what matters is that they're reduced leftovers of an ancestral feature. Another example: the reduced eyes of blind cave fish.

cards.title: According to the biological species concept, what makes two populations members of the same species?
cards.body:
Their members can interbreed in nature and produce viable, fertile offspring, and are reproductively isolated from other such groups.
Limitation: it can't be applied to fossils or to asexual organisms such as prokaryotes, so morphological, ecological and phylogenetic species concepts are used as well.

cards.title: Eastern spotted skunks mate in late winter, western spotted skunks in late summer, so they don't interbreed. Which specific barrier is this?
cards.body:
Temporal isolation, a prezygotic barrier (it acts before fertilization).
Other prezygotic barriers: habitat, behavioral, mechanical and gametic isolation. Postzygotic barriers act after a hybrid zygote forms: reduced hybrid viability, reduced hybrid fertility and hybrid breakdown.

cards.title: A horse and a donkey can produce a mule, but mules are sterile. What type of reproductive barrier is this?
cards.body:
A postzygotic barrier: reduced hybrid fertility.
The hybrid forms and survives but can't reproduce, because the parents' chromosomes differ in number and structure and can't pair properly in meiosis. Other postzygotic barriers: reduced hybrid viability and hybrid breakdown (later-generation hybrids are feeble or sterile).

cards.title: What is the key difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation?
cards.body:
Allopatric: a geographic barrier splits a population and the isolated groups diverge (e.g., snapping shrimp separated by the Isthmus of Panama).
Sympatric: a new species arises within the same area, with no geographic barrier, through polyploidy, habitat differentiation or sexual selection.

cards.title: A cell-division error gives a plant extra chromosome sets, isolating it from its parent species in one generation. What is this condition?
cards.body:
Polyploidy.
A tetraploid (4n) can self-pollinate or mate with other tetraploids, but crosses with its diploid parents give triploid offspring with reduced fertility, so it's reproductively isolated at once. It's a common route to sympatric speciation in plants; wheat, oats, cotton and potatoes are polyploids.

cards.title: Hair is found in all mammals and in no other vertebrates. In cladistic terms, what kind of character is hair for the mammal clade?
cards.body:
A shared derived character (synapomorphy): an evolutionary novelty unique to a clade, so it can define that clade.
A backbone is a shared ancestral character for mammals: it arose in an earlier ancestor and is shared with other vertebrates. A clade is an ancestor plus all of its descendants.

cards.title: How does the punctuated equilibrium model of the tempo of speciation differ from gradualism?
cards.body:
Punctuated equilibrium: species appear relatively suddenly in the fossil record, then change little for long periods (stasis). Gradualism: species diverge slowly and steadily through many intermediate forms.
The fossil record shows both patterns, and 'sudden' in geologic time can still mean tens of thousands of years.

packs.title: Human Physiology
packs.description: Neuron signaling, muscle contraction, blood flow and the pacemaker, the nephron, ADH and aldosterone, glucose control, the Bohr effect, immunity and hormones.

cards.title: Which ion, leaking out through channels that stay open at rest, is mainly responsible for a neuron's negative resting potential?
cards.body:
K⁺ (potassium).
K⁺ is concentrated inside the cell and diffuses out, leaving the inside at about −70 mV (typically −60 to −80 mV). The Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains the gradients: high K⁺ inside, high Na⁺ outside.

cards.title: When a neuron reaches threshold, influx of which ion through voltage-gated channels causes the rising phase of the action potential?
cards.body:
Na⁺ (sodium).
At threshold (often about −55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, making the inside positive. Then Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ flows out (falling phase), and the membrane briefly dips below rest (undershoot). Inactivated Na⁺ channels cause the refractory period, so signals travel one way.

cards.title: In myelinated axons, action potentials are regenerated only at the gaps between myelin segments. What is this jumping conduction called?
cards.body:
Saltatory conduction (Latin saltare, to leap).
The gaps are nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels cluster. Myelin comes from Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS, and makes conduction much faster than in unmyelinated axons of the same diameter. Multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin.

cards.title: When an action potential reaches an axon terminal, influx of which ion triggers synaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitter?
cards.body:
Ca²⁺ (calcium), entering through voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
The vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane (exocytosis), and the neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft to bind receptors, often ligand-gated ion channels, on the postsynaptic cell.

cards.title: In skeletal muscle, Ca²⁺ binds which protein, shifting tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin?
cards.body:
Troponin (the troponin complex).
The Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum after an action potential spreads down the T tubules. Trap: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, not tropomyosin or myosin. When Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin re-blocks the sites and the muscle relaxes.

cards.title: In the cross-bridge cycle, what must bind to a myosin head to make it let go of actin?
cards.body:
ATP.
ATP binding releases the head; hydrolyzing it to ADP and phosphate then cocks the head into its high-energy position, ready to bind actin and pull again (power stroke). With no ATP after death, myosin stays locked to actin: rigor mortis. The filaments slide past each other; neither one shortens.

cards.title: Trace blood through the heart from the venae cavae to the aorta, naming each chamber and valve in order.
cards.body:
Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta.
Trap: pulmonary arteries carry O₂-poor blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its O₂ content.

cards.title: What cluster of specialized cells in the wall of the right atrium sets the heart's rhythm as its pacemaker?
cards.body:
The SA (sinoatrial) node.
Its impulses spread across both atria through gap junctions, are delayed about 0.1 s at the AV node so the atria can empty first, then travel along the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers through the ventricles.

cards.title: Trace filtrate through a nephron, from where it forms to the collecting duct.
cards.body:
Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct.
Blood pressure forces water and small solutes (salts, glucose, amino acids, urea) out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule; cells and large proteins stay in the blood. The loop of Henle (water leaves the descending limb, NaCl the ascending) builds the salty medulla that lets the collecting duct concentrate urine.

cards.title: Which hormone, released from the posterior pituitary when blood osmolarity rises, adds aquaporins to collecting duct cells?
cards.body:
ADH (antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin), made in the hypothalamus.
More aquaporins let the kidney reabsorb more water, concentrating the urine and bringing blood osmolarity back down (negative feedback). Alcohol inhibits ADH release, producing dilute urine.

cards.title: Which adrenal hormone, triggered by the renin–angiotensin system, makes the distal tubule and collecting duct reabsorb more Na⁺?
cards.body:
Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex.
Low blood pressure or volume makes the juxtaglomerular apparatus release renin, leading to angiotensin II, which stimulates the adrenal cortex. Reabsorbing more Na⁺ (with water following) raises blood volume and pressure. ADH, by contrast, mainly controls water alone.

cards.title: When blood glucose falls between meals, which hormone from pancreatic alpha cells raises it back toward its set point?
cards.body:
Glucagon: it signals the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose.
After a meal, beta cells release insulin, which helps body cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen. Each hormone's effect reverses the change that triggered it: negative feedback.

cards.title: Lower pH from CO₂ in active tissues reduces hemoglobin's affinity for O₂, so it unloads more O₂. What is this called?
cards.body:
The Bohr effect (Bohr shift): the O₂ dissociation curve shifts right.
CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, releasing H⁺ that binds hemoglobin and changes its shape. Each hemoglobin has 4 subunits, each with an iron-containing heme that binds one O₂, and binding is cooperative, giving an S-shaped curve.

cards.title: How does innate immunity differ from adaptive immunity in speed, specificity and memory?
cards.body:
Innate: rapid, recognizes molecules shared by broad groups of pathogens (e.g., via Toll-like receptors), no memory. Includes barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells and inflammation; found in all animals.
Adaptive: slower first response, highly specific B- and T-cell receptors, and immunological memory; vertebrates only.

cards.title: What does each do: B cells, helper T cells (CD4) and cytotoxic T cells (CD8)?
cards.body:
B cells: become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral response).
Helper T (CD4): recognize antigen on class II MHC of antigen-presenting cells, then release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. HIV destroys them.
Cytotoxic T (CD8): recognize antigen on class I MHC and kill infected or cancer cells with perforin and granzymes.

cards.title: Why do steroid hormones bind receptors inside target cells, while peptide hormones like insulin bind receptors on the surface?
cards.body:
Steroids (e.g., cortisol, estradiol) are lipid-soluble: they diffuse through the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors, and the hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor.
Peptide hormones are water-soluble and can't cross the membrane, so they bind surface receptors that trigger signal transduction, often via second messengers like cAMP.
